vignette:
Leilani was nineteen when it happened, though she seldom speaks of that night in any form that holds together. She had been with him for almost a year, a man a few years older who she'd met through friends. He was charming at first, then possessive, then something else entirely. The evening that ended everything started over a disagreement about dinner—she couldn't remember the specifics, only the way his voice rose, the way he shoved her backward into the bedroom, and then the dark. He had flipped the light switch as he came after her, and the rest unfolded in blackness punctuated by sharp sounds: his palm against her cheek, the crack of her head against the wall, his breathing, her own choking sobs. When it was over, she lay on the floor for hours, too afraid to move, too afraid to turn the light back on and see her own face in the mirror.

In the weeks that followed, Leilani told herself she should have left earlier, should have known, should have spoken up before it got that far. She replayed the arguments, the warning signs she had ignored, and each time the guilt landed in her chest like a stone. When a close friend asked what happened, Leilani opened her mouth but the words scattered—she could not hold the sequence, could not make the beginning lead to the end, and eventually she just shook her head and stopped trying. Worse were the moments when the terror would wash over her without warning, without any image attached, as if her body remembered something her mind had misplaced. She would be sitting at her drafting table, focused on a client's color palette, and suddenly she was trembling, her heart hammering, and she had no idea why. Then, about three months after the assault, she saw him. She was at a small grocery store near her apartment, reaching for a carton of milk, when he rounded the end of the aisle. He was wearing the same jacket, walking with the same easy confidence, and for a split second their eyes met. Leilani dropped the milk. The glass shattered, but she did not hear it—she only felt her legs carry her out of the store, past the register, into the parking lot, where she crouched behind a car and shook until the manager came out to check on her. She never went back to that store. After that, she began scanning every crowd, every parking lot, certain he would appear again. She took longer routes home, avoided the neighborhood where he lived, and stopped going out after dark altogether.

By the time she met her husband a year later, she had convinced herself that the past was over. She married quickly, wanting to feel safe, wanting to belong somewhere. But safety proved elusive. Her interior design work required her to meet clients in empty rooms, to walk through half-built spaces alone, and she found herself scheduling every appointment for midday when the light was fullest, when other people were nearby. She stopped taking evening consultations altogether. When male clients or contractors asked for a private walkthrough, she invented reasons for an assistant to come along, or she cancelled. One important client—a developer building a custom home—insisted on a late-afternoon meeting to review lighting options in the basement. Leilani could not explain why she refused; she simply said she was unavailable, and the client moved on. She lost the contract, but what frightened her most was not the lost income. It was the way her body had gone rigid the moment she imagined standing in that dark, unfinished room with a man she did not know.

She began to notice other patterns. She could not tolerate loud noises—a car backfiring on the street, a door slamming in the office—without her entire frame going tight, without scanning the room for an exit. She checked behind her constantly, even at home, even when her husband stood two feet away. She avoided being alone in any room with any man, including her own husband if the lights were dim or the door was closed. He did not understand why she flinched when he came up behind her, why she insisted on keeping every lamp on at night. She did not have the words to tell him, because when she tried, the story fell apart again—the thread lost, the guilt rising, the emotion outpacing any memory. Once, driving home from work, she thought she spotted him at a crosswalk—a man with the same build, the same stride—and she swerved into a side street, her heart hammering, and sat there for ten minutes before she could breathe normally again. She was certain she was being watched, that he was looking for her, that she would never be truly safe.

Now, at twenty, Leilani sits in a therapist's office for the first time. She came because she is exhausted, because her marriage is fraying, because she no longer recognizes the person she has become. She is certain her life has been destroyed, that she no longer belongs anywhere—not in her own home, not among friends, not even inside her own skin. She trusts no one, least of all herself. What she hopes for, though she can barely say it aloud, is that someone might help her find a way back to the light, and that she might one day walk into a room without first checking who is behind her, and that she might one day pass a stranger on the street without seeing his face.
